title: Kuli-Kuli
author: Fran Osseo-Asare
desc: A cup of roasted peanuts ground to a paste, the oil pressed out between two cutting boards through cloth, then deep-fried until crisp and brown.
longDesc: Kuli-kuli is a peanut snack and the reason it matters beyond itself is that pressing the oil out is what makes tankora powder possible. A cup of dry roasted unsalted peanuts is ground, the powder is wrapped in cloth, and the oil is pressed out between two cutting boards. A little hot water is added to bring it together, and the shapes are deep-fried in hot peanut oil for a few minutes until crisp and brown on the outside. The result is both a snack in its own right and the de-oiled peanut that chichinga's coating depends on.
ingredients: Salt, ground chilli or ginger, to taste
steps: Grind the dry roasted peanuts to a powder or paste.
Press the oil out between two cutting boards.
Add a little hot water to bring the de-oiled paste together.
Shape into small sticks, rings or balls.
Deep-fry in hot peanut oil a few minutes, until crisp and brown on the outside.
// For tankora powder: grind the finished kuli-kuli to a powder. See GHA064.
chefTips: Pressing the oil out is the whole technique and it is harder work than it sounds. Cloth, two boards, and real pressure.
Save the pressed oil. It is fragrant roasted groundnut oil and it is good for frying the kuli-kuli itself.
A little hot water, not cold. The warmth helps the de-oiled paste bind rather than crumble.
Crisp and brown on the outside is the frying cue, within a few minutes. The inside stays denser.
Dry roasted and UNSALTED. Salted peanuts will make the finished kuli-kuli and any tankora from it too salty to control.
This is the prerequisite for tankora powder — the de-oiled peanut is what keeps the spice blend a dry powder instead of turning to butter. See GHA064.
Kuli-kuli is eaten on its own across West Africa, crumbled over salads and porridges, and ground into spice blends. It is more useful than it looks.
commonMistakes: Not pressing out enough oil, so the paste will not hold or grind.
Frying too long, which makes them hard rather than crisp.
sources: Adapted from 'Recipes #39 and 40: Kuli kuli and tankora', betumiblog.blogspot.com, Wednesday 3 February 2010. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Posted by Fran at 4:43 PM'. Quantities confirmed across two fetches (TWO-PASS).

Ingredients and method as printed: '1 cup dry roasted unsalted peanuts'; 'Wrap the powder in cloth, and press the oil out between 2 cutting boards'; add a little hot water; 'Deepfried them in hot peanut oil for a few minutes until they were crisp and brown on the outside.'
DONENESS CUE, as printed: 'crisp and brown on the outside', within 'a few minutes'.
NO YIELD is printed. The six servings above is an editorial reading of a cup of peanuts.
NO SHAPING INSTRUCTION is given in the source — kuli-kuli is made in sticks, rings and balls across West Africa, and the step above offers those without attributing them to this source.

THE OPTIONAL SEASONINGS in the ingredient list are NOT in the source, which gives peanuts, hot water and frying oil only. They are listed as optional and flagged here as an editorial addition reflecting common practice, not the author's.

ITS ROLE AS A PREREQUISITE: the tankora powder at GHA064, from the same post, calls for '1/2 cup powdered peanuts from kulikuli'. That dependency is why this entry is published — without the de-oiled peanut the spice blend does not work, and the source treats them as a pair.
SAVING THE PRESSED OIL is not stated by the source; it follows from the process and is offered in the tips as practice rather than instruction.
ON THE NAME: kuli-kuli is eaten across West Africa and the name is the same in Hausa, Yoruba and Ghanaian usage. It is the same product that goes into Nigerian yaji.
storage: 2 weeks in an airtight tin once fully cool.
reheating: A low oven briefly to re-crisp.
healthBenefits: Very high in protein once the oil is pressed out.
Pressing removes a large share of the fat.
Peanuts supply niacin, folate, magnesium and vitamin E.
culturalNote: Kuli-kuli is sold in little stacks at markets from Senegal to Cameroon and it is one of the oldest documented processed foods in the region — a way of making peanuts keep, travel and turn into a dry spice powder, all from one press between two boards.
